COP31 ends without deal after climate change talks break down C By Courtney Gould
The COP31 UN climate summit has ended without a deal after debate broke down over a draft which failed to mention fossil fuels.

The main deal was rejected on Sunday afternoon, local time, by a host of nations, 44 hours after the summit's official close and following two weeks of negotiations. It marked the longest UN climate summit ever.

In a chaotic finale to the talks in the Turkish city of Antalya, debate continued in overtime until COP31 presidents Australia and Türkiye confirmed they would not put forward another draft of the deal.

Several countries and the 27-nation European Union said they could not accept the final proposal from the joint Turkish-Australian leadership that did not mention fossil fuels, slamming it as too weak.

"We will not endorse a cover decision … that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change," said Ireland's climate minister, Darragh O'Brien, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency.

items.title: Australia's neighbour claims 'China, Russia' looking at oil and gas project
paras: Woodside left the Greater Sunrise project last month, and analysts say it could lead Timor-Leste to bankruptcy. ( ABC News: Margaret Burin )

Timor-Leste's government is claiming Russian and Chinese companies have expressed an interest in its multi-billion-dollar Greater Sunrise oil and gas project, as it continues to doggedly pursue its development despite all major companies now abandoning it.

It comes as one leading analyst says the country's current pathway with the project will either be a "diabolical disaster" leading to financial ruin, or force Timor-Leste to "cede its economic sovereignty" to a country such as China to get it over the line.

The oil and gas project, which sits 500km north of Darwin, was thrown into turmoil last month when Australian oil and gas giant Woodside sold its 33.4 per cent stake back to Timor-Leste, effectively handing the government full control of its future development.

The Timorese government has banked its entire economic future on Greater Sunrise, with the government already spending almost $2 billion on building infrastructure in preparation for a proposed pipeline and buying out major gas companies.

The country, one of the poorest in south-east Asia, wants to build its own oil and gas industry and is insisting the gas from the project be piped to Timor, rather than the cheaper option through existing infrastructure to Darwin.

Earlier this month, the country's prime minister Xanana Gusmao attended a ceremony in the capital Dili, pressing the go button for a submarine that will map the sea floor to choose a route for the proposed pipeline.
The submarine the Timor-Leste government launched to map the seafloor for the Greater Sunrise project. ( ABC News: Vonia Vieira )
At the ceremony, Timor-Leste's Petroleum Minister Francisco da Costa Monteiro told the ABC the project will happen.
"We have no doubt the Greater Sunrise can be developed in the near future," he said.
"This field remains very attractive, not just for Timor-Leste, but also for the other potential players in the region and in the world."
This four-lane expressway was constructed almost a decade ago. ( ABC News: Vonia Vieira )
He said a number of unnamed companies, including those from Russia and China, had already approached them following Woodside's exit.

"We cannot say A-B-C, but certainly there's companies in the region, as well as far as other parts of the world … in Europe, America, and in Russia, in China, in Japan. There are quite a number of parties we've been engaging."
But analysts have long questioned the viability of the project and the government's insistence on processing the gas in the country's south.
MST Financial's Saul Kavonic, a leading oil and gas analyst, told the ABC the country had "good reasons" to bring the gas to Timor and build its own industry.
But, he said, the small size of the resource compared to other deposits around the world meant the commercial realities of Greater Sunrise did not stack up.
"I really hope they prove my view — and that of many others in the industry who have similar views — wrong.
"The fact is that the Timorese government has got its heels so dug in on this issue [of processing in Timor] that it does threaten the ongoing viability of the nation going forward."
Mr Kavonic said the fact that all four major oil and gas companies previously involved in Greater Sunrise had now left the project highlighted its lack of commercial appeal.
Oil and gas analyst Saul Kavonic believes there only a handful of options to save the Greater Sunrise project. ( ABC News )
Responding to the Timorese government's claim that it had interests from a number of companies, including those from Russia and China, Mr Kavonic said the Russian scenario was "unlikely".
But, he said, the China option was one of the limited pathways that may see it succeed.

"That is one of the big concerns here, in that in its pursuit of trying to get this project done they ultimately have to resort to ceding part of their economic sovereignty to another nation like China."
The overall development cost of Greater Sunrise has not been disclosed.

One 2015 report indicated it would cost $US20.5 billion ($29 billion) to develop in Timor, while a counter report commissioned by the Timor-Leste government in 2021 declared it would cost $US14.1 billion ($21.1 billion).

Timor-Leste has a sovereign wealth fund with about $US18 billion ($27 billion) remaining, according to Timor's central bank , but the gas project that was providing royalties to it is no longer operational.

With labour and construction costs now drastically more expensive, most analysts expect that the country would have to dip into a substantial chunk of its sovereign wealth fund for Greater Sunrise to become a reality.
The map shows the location of the Greater Sunrise project within the Timor Sea between Australia and Timor-Leste. ( Supplied: DFAT )
The Timor-Leste government told the ABC it was aiming to fund Greater Sunrise via 30 per cent "equity" and 70 per cent "project finance".
Marta Da Silva, the head of Timor local government accountability organisation La'o Hamutuk, said the country was in danger of falling off a "fiscal cliff".
Marta Da Silva is the head of local NGO La'o Hamutuk. ( ABC News: Nick Sas )
"The question [is] where the government is getting the money to fund this project?" she said.
"With Greater Sunrise, we cannot only speak about [our] sovereignty as a country, but we must look at the economy, how viable [it is] and how the people can get the benefits from those industries."

items.title: Giants clash over Australia's gas reservation policy
paras: Santos has been accused of taking gas out of the domestic market instead of supplying it. ( ABC News )
It was, according to Queensland Coalition senator Susan McDonald, a "most unsatisfactory" mistake.
The Senate was interrogating the federal government's plans for a domestic gas reservation scheme, and bitter rivals had accidentally been lumped together to appear at the same time.
In one corner was Dan Clark, the head of giant east coast gas exporter Australia Pacific LNG (APLNG).

In the other was Tracey Winters, chief strategy officer of Australia's second-biggest oil and gas company, Santos, the operator of a neighbouring plant on Queensland's Curtis Island known as Gladstone LNG (GLNG).
Mr Clark pointed out that APLNG had supplied the equivalent of four years of the eastern states' entire domestic gas demand since starting operations 10 years ago.
By contrast, and in none-too-subtle terms, he said, "another" player had taken almost as much gas out of the domestic market.
"Since the startup of our LNG facility, APLNG has delivered over 1,900 petajoules to the domestic market," Mr Clark told the Senate's Economics Legislation Committee.
"But for every four of those petajoules APLNG has contributed to Australia, another exporter on the east coast has taken three petajoules back out."
Dan Clark and Tracey Winters gave evidence to the Senate regarding the reservation scheme. ( Supplied )
"In the evidence that we just heard, APLNG is acting purely in its commercial interests," she argued.
That the two were exchanging home truths is testament to how heated the debate about gas reservation on the east coast has become and how high the stakes have risen.
In the normally clubby and civilised world of Australia's oil and gas industry, relations between some of its biggest players have descended into open conflict.
On one side is APLNG and its partners, led by Australian energy giant Origin and US major ConocoPhillips.
It is joined by British-Dutch company Shell, which operates the third of the east coast gas exporters, Queensland Curtis LNG (QCLNG), along with users and many industry observers.
But on the other side is Santos, the country's mid-sized gas producer, and the foreign interests that have invested in GLNG and are banking on the gas it can provide them.
Adelaide-based Santos has pushed heavily into exports through projects like GLNG. ( ABC News: Che Chorley )
Josh Stabler, the founder of consultancy Energy Edge, said the dispute playing out publicly had been going on privately for years.
"It does appear that now that there's been legislative shifts, it's become more public in terms of the concerns," Mr Stabler said.
At the heart of the dispute, he said, was a fundamental mismatch between the three east coast exporters and what they were providing to the local market.
Whereas APLNG and QCLNG had more than enough gas to run their export plants at capacity and supply plenty of gas to domestic users, it was a very different story for Santos and its partners.
To plug the gap, he said GLNG had consistently sucked up huge volumes of gas from the domestic market so it could be sold overseas.
"It is certainly taking a large amount of gas, be it under long-term foundational contracts or short-term ones, to meet its LNG exports."
Research from Energy Edge reveals Santos has taken much of this gas from the Cooper Basin, a vast onshore gas field operated by Santos in outback South Australia and Queensland.
Historically, it was one of the biggest sources of supply to South Australia and New South Wales.
The Moomba gas field, tapped to supply the domestic market, is in outback South Australia. ( ABC News: Mike Sexton )
But that all changed in 2016, when Santos began sending 140 terajoules a day from the basin north to its export facility at Gladstone.
The east coast domestic gas market uses about 1,400 terajoules of gas a day.
Despite assurances to the market operator in 2013 that production from the basin would increase to 600 terajoules a day, more than compensating for export volumes, output has instead declined.
Since GLNG started, Santos has diverted more than half of the gas produced in the Cooper Basin to exports.
Mr Stabler says the Cooper Basin is the most obvious example of Santos depleting the local market for its export needs, but there are others.
Among them is a contract the company signed with AGL last decade, described by others as a sellout of Australian gas consumers.
The gas was originally sold to AGL by Shell, which signed a 20-year deal at discounted prices to ensure domestic consumers could get access to affordable supplies.
However, AGL, under controversial former chief Andy Vesey, flipped the contract to Santos in 2015.
The deal locked in profits for AGL but deprived local consumers of huge volumes of gas which were then exported through GLNG.
"It certainly doesn't look good in retrospect, that deal," Mr Stabler said.
Santos has repeatedly stated the contract with AGL will not be renewed when it expires at the end of next year.
The company has also noted GLNG is no longer buying gas from Origin, an arrangement that finished at the end of last year, since when prices local prices have eased.
Ms Winters has argued it is not correct to suggest Santos has been depleting the local market, saying the company had supplied the equivalent of 26 per cent of its export volumes to the east coast.

"The east coast gas market … faces future projected shortfalls … because of the failure of state governments in New South Wales and Victoria to facilitate the development of their gas resources for the last 15 years," Ms Winters told the committee.
Under the Commonwealth's plans, gas exporters would be required to supply the equivalent of up to 20 per cent of their annual production to the domestic market.
The scheme would be aimed at ensuring producers supplied 110 per cent of forecast demand to put downward pressure on prices.
But with federal parliament likely to pass the legislation underpinning the scheme in the coming days, analysts are warning it is still riddled with shortcomings.
Inpex is celebrating its 100th LNG shipment from Darwin. ( Supplied: Inpex )
Hamish McKenzie, the deputy director of climate change and energy at the Grattan Institute, said the government's oversupply target of 110 per cent of demand was too much.
"A big oversupply risks tanking the domestic gas sector and pushing up gas prices," Mr McKenzie wrote on social media.
"A straightforward solution would be to amend the legislation to cap the oversupply at a much smaller level: we have suggested 2 to 5 [per cent]."
In its testimony before the Senate, Shell echoed Mr McKenzie's comments, while saying a domestic reservation scheme "overall … would be a good thing for Australia".

But Cameron Crowther, Shell's general manager of growth and strategy in Australia, said that, because the company had been a long-term supplier to the local market, "must-sell" provisions were unnecessary, as was the possibility of prosecution.
However, in a veiled swipe at GLNG and Santos, he warned the government against playing favourites or exempting producers from providing their fair share of supply.
"The problem is that the granting of exemption or variation for one exporter in the way the bill is drafted simply transfers that obligation onto other exporters," Mr Crowther said.

"What that means for Shell and our partners … who have consistently and voluntarily made good on our commitment to the domestic market, is that we're left uncertain as to what the ongoing commitment is going to need to be."
Independent senator David Pocock was more blunt, using his additional comments in the Senate inquiry report into the scheme to argue Santos and GLNG must not be allowed to "avoid their obligations".
According to Senator Pocock, the bill contained "loopholes" that could let Santos slip free "through accounting arrangements that leave Australian consumers no better off".
David Pocock is demanding more safeguards to avoid lobbying from gas companies. ( ABC News: David Sciasci )
Crucially, he said it appeared the legislation would do little to prevent a gas exporter from acquiring a domestic gas producer or field and counting the production towards their quota.
"Compliance must be based on a real increase in gas available to the domestic market."
And he said the discretion available to the minister risked turning the scheme into a "lobbyists' picnic unless there are appropriate safeguards".

While Senator Pocock stressed the policy should go hand in hand with a gas export tax to ensure Australians received a better return on the sale of their resources, he said it should not be used to foster increased gas production.

A Santos spokeswoman said Senator Pocock's arguments would make it virtually impossible for the company to meet its domestic obligations without breaking its long-term contracts with overseas customers.
"Senator Pocock's recommended amendments to the bill make clear his aim is to shut down the gas industry," the spokeswoman said.
Josh Stabler said the spectacle of huge corporate interests duking it out would normally not concern consumers.
But it was different when they were caught in the melee because they were in the fight over gas supplies.

items.title: Council allows private land burials for those who 'belong to the land'
paras: Major 'Moogy' Sumner at the burial site of his brother at the Coorong. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara )
Coorong District Council has approved a new policy for burials on private land.
Family farms are among the eligible sites with fewer preservation rights than a cemetery.
The Aboriginal Lands Trust says burials on land it manages will never be dug up.
A coffin strapped to the sidecar of a Harley-Davidson recently roared through SA's south-east, leading a sea of fellow motorcyclists through the Coorong.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the name of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of family.
In the coffin was Basil "Mulla" Sumner, and he was being taken to a quiet, windswept area overlooking the estuary.
The funeral procession ended on a scenic plot in Dupang, around a half-hour drive from the nearest cemetery.
His brother, Major "Moogy" Sumner, said it had been his brother's wish to be returned where they "grew up here as kids running around … our traditional land".
Moogy Sumner grew up metres away from where his brother was buried nine weeks ago. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara )
"[Mulla] said, 'When I pass away, I want to go back to Dupang, and I want to get buried right next to where our dad was born," Mr Sumner said, a Ngarrindjeri and Kaurna man — like his brother.

Mr Sumner's wish was made possible by approval from the Coorong District Council, the latest in South Australia to green light a policy for private land burials, following similar moves at Yankalilla and Mount Remarkable.
While there are relatively few regulations around where ashes are spread after we die, the legislation for burials on private property differs between Australian states and territories.
In South Australia, local councils determine private burials, provided the proposed site is located in an area outside a township or Metropolitan Adelaide and other stipulations.

Coorong District Council's burial policy rules out private properties inside town boundaries, which means only large areas, such as family farms and areas managed by the Aboriginal Lands Trust (ALT), are eligible to apply.
Jonathan Pietzsch says councillors received private land burial requests "a couple of times a year". ( Supplied )
Among other conditions, burials must be publicly recorded, cannot be within 20 metres of any structure and cannot risk polluting waterways.
The niche policy has caused some community unease, with fears that human remains could eventually be dug up or disturbed.
The policy states private plots are not the same as a cemetery and "therefore have no preservation rights".
"There's been that one concern — what happens if a property is sold?" said Coorong's Deputy Mayor Jonathan Pietzsch.
While that remained a real risk for farm burials, sites managed by the ALT had stronger protections, according to chief executive of South Australia Kerri Wilson said.
Kerri Wilson says there are "safeguards" for Aboriginal Lands Trust sites. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara )
"Legislation allows our people to be returned to these parcels of land, never to be dug up or removed again."
Sam Dodd's family has been farming in the Coorong region since 1859; the property is seemingly an ideal fit for a burial request.
"It's certainly a subject we've discussed as a family," the fifth-generation farmer said.
Mr Dodd said while he did feel a connection to the land, it was "in no way" comparable to First Nation's people.
Sam Dodd said there was "little point" of a farm burial if it was going to be sold. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara )
Mr Dodd believed a visible grave site on the farm would bring "negative vibes" and leaned towards a somewhat novel cremation method.
"My plan is to get mixed up with my ashes in multiple tonnes of fertiliser so I can be spread far and wide so I have quite a connection over a large piece of property," he said.
Mr Dodd said there needed to be a way to prove families have a long-term connection, but there was "little point" in a farm burial if it was going to be sold.
The private burial policy states council must consider the likelihood of remains being disturbed and has the "absolute discretion" to deem a site unsuitable for human remains.
Cr Pietzsch said the policy will also allow for the repatriation of Aboriginal remains.
He believed councillors would look back in several decades "and go, 'Yeah, I'm really glad we did it'."
Moogy hopes his father's remains can be exhumed from Adelaide and reburied alongside Mulla. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara )
Mr Sumner said his family had always had a connection to the Coorong site where his brother now lay.
"The sand hills over there, the Southern Ocean … that's always been a part of our life," the Ngarrindjeri Kaurna man said.
Following the new policy, he planned to have his dad moved from the West Terrace Cemetery in Adelaide to join Mulla Sumner.

items.title: Reserve Bank issues Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) (Second Amendment) Regulations
paras: The Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2015 were superseded by the Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026, which were issued on January 13, 2026 , and became effective from October 01, 2026. The new regulations are principle based; intended to promote ease of doing business, especially for small exporters and importers; and empower Authorised Dealers to provide quicker and more efficient service to their customers. Based on subsequent feedback received from stakeholders, the Reserve Bank has issued Amendment Regulations to Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026 that were notified on November 02, 2026 , and came into effect, retrospectively, from October 01, 2026 . In this regard, to facilitate better understanding of the new trade regulations by the exporters/importers and other stakeholders, the Reserve Bank has placed a Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on the Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026 on its website. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1531

items.title: RBI imposes monetary penalty on Fusion Finance Limited
paras: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has, by an order dated November 17, 2026, imposed a monetary penalty of ₹7.50 lakh (Rupees Seven Lakh Fifty Thousand only) on Fusion Finance Limited (the company) for non-compliance with certain provisions of directions issued by RBI on ‘Know Your Customer (KYC)’ and ‘Internal Ombudsman’. This penalty has been imposed in exercise of powers conferred on RBI under section 58G(1)(b) read with section 58B(5)(aa) of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. The statutory inspection of the company was conducted by RBI with reference to its financial position as on March 31, 2026. Based on the supervisory findings of non-compliance with RBI directions and related correspondence in that regard, a notice was issued to the company advising it to show cause as to why penalty should not be imposed on it for failure to comply with the RBI directions. After considering the company's reply to the notice, additional submissions made by it and oral submissions made during the personal hearing, RBI found that the following charges against the company were sustained, warranting imposition of monetary penalty: The company failed to obtain PAN or equivalent e-document thereof or Form 60 from customers, while establishing an account-based relationship with those customers; and, The company failed to escalate the partly or wholly rejected complaints to the Internal Ombudsman for a final decision within the prescribed time. This action is based on deficiencies in regulatory compliance and is not intended to pronounce upon the validity of any transaction or agreement entered into by the company with its customers. Further, imposition of this monetary penalty is without prejudice to any other action that may be initiated by RBI against the company. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1537

items.title: Indian students in Kazan delighted as PM Modi arrives for BRICS Summit
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel Kazan [ Russia ], October 22 (ANI): Indian students in Kazan , Russia , are happy and excited about Prime Minister Narendra Modi's arrival at Hotel Korston , as he attends the 16th BRICS Summit . Notably, PM Narendra Modi on Tuesday touched down in Kazan city of Russia to participate in the 16th BRICS Summit and received a warm welcome. He is here to attend the 16th BRICS Summit , being held under the Chairmanship of Russia . To welcome PM Modi , students from India studying in Russia also sang a welcome song as they awaited PM Modi 's arrival at Hotel Korston . An Indian student from Pune, Saniya said that the students are quite excited to greet PM Modi . "Maybe we will get the opportunity (to meet PM Modi ) as many students are here (at Hotel Korston )... We are very excited. We are lucky to have this opportunity and we are happy to see him," she told ANI. An Indian student from Bihar, Shaurya Pratap said, "We are very happy to welcome PM Modi and we have prepared a song for him and we hope he likes it." Surbhi from Delhi said, "I have been here in Kazan since 2019 and today, we are going to sing a song for PM Modi and we are very excited about that." Parul, a final-year medical student, who has been in Kazan for the last five years told ANI, "We are really grateful that we got this opportunity to welcome our dear Prime Minister." Arti Pawar from Maharashtra said, "I have been living here for the past three years. I am very happy that PM Modi is coming here." Mrunmayi from Nagpur, Maharashtra said, "All the students here are quite enthusiastic as PM is going to come soon. We are too much delighted to welcome him." Meanwhile, ISKCON volunteers - from the Russia n and Indian communities were seen chanting 'Hare Krishna, Hare Ram' ahead of PM Modi 's arrival. While speaking with ANI, Sergoy, an ISKCON volunteer, said, "'Hare Krishna is a Mahamantra. This visit of PM Modi to Kazan , Russia is an important one for us. We are happy." Another ISKCON volunteer said, "We want to welcome PM Modi here in Kazan . It's a great honour for us to welcome him here We are very excited to see him." A Russia n citizen, Alexander said that the people there will welcome PM Modi by singing a song and that he is happy with PM Modi 's visit to Kazan . He said, "We have made a banner and we will also sing a song to welcome PM Modi ... I returned from India just two days back and directly came from Delhi to Kazan to see PM Modi . I am very happy that he is coming to Russia ." Notably, ahead of his departure to Russia , PM Modi shared a post on X and wrote, "Leaving for Kazan , Russia , to take part in the BRICS Summit . India attaches immense importance to BRICS, and I look forward to extensive discussions on a wide range of subjects. I also look forward to meeting various leaders there." The Prime Minister's office in a statement quoted PM Modi as saying, "I am departing today on a two-day visit to Kazan at the invitation of H.E. Mr. Vladimir Putin, President of the Russia n Federation, to attend the 16th BRICS Summit ." "India values the close cooperation within BRICS which has emerged as an important platform for dialogue and discussion on issues concerning the global developmental agenda, reformed multilateralism, climate change, economic cooperation, building resilient supply chains, promoting cultural and people to people connect, among others," PM Modi said. The statement further said that the expansion of BRICS with the addition of new members last year has added to its inclusivity and agenda for the global good. "Building upon the Annual Summit held in July 2024 in Moscow, my visit to Kazan will further reinforce the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between India and Russia . I look forward to meeting other leaders from BRICS as well," the PMO statement said. The 16th BRICS Summit in Kazan is being held under the chairmanship of Russia from October 22-24. During his visit, PM Modi is also expected to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts from BRICS member countries and invited leaders in Kazan . The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said, "The Summit, themed 'Strengthening Multilateralism for Just Global Development and Security,' will provide an important platform for leaders to discuss key global issues." It further said, "The Summit will offer a valuable opportunity to assess the progress of initiatives launched by BRICS and to identify potential areas for future collaboration." This visit marks, PM Modi 's second visit to Russia this year. He travelled to Moscow in July to attend the 22nd India- Russia Annual Summit where he held a bilateral meeting with President Putin. He was also conferred with Russia 's highest civilian award, the Order of St. Andrew the Apostle at the Kremlin in Moscow. BRIC, as a formal grouping, started after the meeting of the Leaders of Russia , India and China in St Petersburg on the margins of G8 Outreach Summit in 2006. The grouping was formalized during the first meeting of BRIC Foreign Ministers on the margins of UNGA in New York in 2006. The first BRIC Summit was held in Russia 's Yekaterinburg in 2009. It was agreed to expand BRIC into BRICS with the inclusion of South Africa at the BRIC Foreign Ministers' meeting in New York in 2010. South Africa attended the 3rd BRICS Summit in Sanya in 2011. A further expansion of BRICS took place in 2024 with five new members - Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. (ANI)

items.title: "Singapore plays key role in Act-East policy": Rajnath Singh at India-Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [ India ], October 22 (ANI): Dr. Ng Eng Hen , Singapore 's Minister of Defence , has begun his three-day visit to India . As part of his visit, Dr. Hen co-chaired the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi, with his India n counterpart Rajnath Singh . The Summit began on Tuesday morning, with India n Defence Minister Rajnath Singh welcoming the Singapore delegation warmly. He noted that the strategic partnership the two countries share is a "testimony of increasing closeness between our countries." Singh said, " The meeting is happening at a time when India marks the decade of India 's Act in Policy, in which Singapore has played a key role in promoting economic cooperation, cultural ties, and developed strategic connectivity with country institutions." Building upon Singh's remarks, Dr. Ng Eng Hen said, "You reminded us that this is the 10th year since your Act East Policy. From Singapore 's perspective, India has always been part of the East. Whether you choose to act or look, we consider you part of the area." He said that while remembering the history of Singapore , India has been an important partner. " When we started the Singapore armed forces, one of the countries that we asked early on to see whether they could help us was India ." Hen highlighted that such historical memoirs serve as important reminders and "reflects how we feel that India is very part of our area. We are delighted that our ten years of bilateral relations have been very much improved in defence and all-round strategic partnership." Hen also thanked PM Modi for visiting Singapore earlier this year and noted that the visit was an excellent meeting. A day before, the Ministry of Defence had announced the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi on October 22, 2024. The release noted that between India and Singapore , "The engagements have diversified to include wide-ranging contacts between the Services, military-to-military exchanges, high-level visits, capacity building and training programs, cooperation in UN Peacekeeping, ship visits and bilateral exercises." Inaugurated in 2016, the India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue is a key platform to strengthen bilateral defence cooperation between Singapore and India . The fifth edition of the Defence Ministers' Dialogue took place in January 2021 through virtual teleconference. During the meeting, the two parties showed confidence in the outcomes of the meeting that would result in providing impetus to the entire spectrum of the bilateral engagement as well as to the regional security architecture. (ANI)

items.title: "High probability of meeting between PM Modi, President Xi": Former Indian envoy on patrolling agreement between India-C
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [ India ], October 22 (ANI): Gautam Bambawale , former India n Ambassador to China , Bhutan, and Pakistan said that the recent agreement on border patrolling between India and China along the Line of Actual Control ( LAC ) has opened up possibilities for a bilateral meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping in Kazan along the sidelines of the BRICS Summit and asserted that the probability of a meeting between the two leaders is "very high." He also noted that although India and China reached an agreement on patrolling arrangements ahead of the BRICS Summit in Kazan , Russia , this breakthrough is the result of discussions and negotiations between India and China , with no involvement from Russia . While speaking with ANI, Bambawale said, "On this question of the recent agreement on patrolling along the LAC , especially in eastern Ladakh, I do not think the Russia ns must have had a hand in it. It would have been discussions between India and China and negotiations between India and China that led to this agreement." He added, "Now that the problems on the border along the LAC have been sorted out, I think there is a very high probability that our Prime Minister Modi and the President of China , Xi Jinping , could have a bilateral meeting in Kazan . I think it would be a meeting to break the ice. I don't expect some great warmth suddenly. It will take time to rebuild the relationship from the setback that it had in the Summer of 2020. This situation has gone on for 4.5 years. So it will take some time to repair the relationship but I think this agreement will be a start and if there's a meeting between the two leaders at the summit level in Kazan on the sidelines of BRICS, then that will be another step towards restoring the relationship to what it was earlier." Bambawale further said that the agreement on patrolling arrangements implies that China is willing to restore the relationship between the two nations to its pre-2020 state, paving the way for progress in other sectors such as trade, commerce, and investment.

He said, "The agreement has come just before the BRICS summit takes place in the next few days in Kazan in Russia . I think what this implies is that the Chinese side is wanting to restore the relationship between India and China to what it was earlier. It wants the other aspects of the relationship like trade, commerce and investment to move ahead. It will of course take some time to restore the trust between the two countries. But at least I think a beginning can be made and perhaps there might be a meeting at the topmost level between PM Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping at Kazan ." The former India n Ambassador further noted that the agreement between India and China is expected to significantly boost the BRICS grouping, despite not necessarily indicating a closer relationship between India and Russia or China . "I won't say India is moving closer to Russia and China but I think the BRICS grouping will be immeasurably strengthened because of this understanding between India and China because of the cooling of tensions on the border between India and China and as India has always said that a peaceful border means that the rest of the relatrionship can also move ahead. So I believe that a better relationship between India and China will be better for the BRICS grouping," Bambawale told ANI. Bambawale further said, "If this implies that the status quo ante has been restored as it existed before the Chinese undertook the military action in eastern Ladakh in summer of 2020... then I think this is a very welcome development. The government of India should be congratulated on taking a firm position on this matter and that India 's stand has been vindicated after 4.5 years of face-to-face situation between India n and Chinese troops. If it means that the status quo ante has been restored, then we definitely welcome this agreement. It is a good agreement and we can move forward on the basis of this agreement." Notably, a day before, Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri, who addressed a special media briefing ahead of PM Modi 's visit to Russia for the BRICS Summit , said India and China have reached an agreement on the patrolling arrangements along LAC . The agreement was reached ahead of the BRICS Summit which will be attended by PM Modi and Chinese President Xi. "On several areas along the Line of Actual Control , we held discussions with Chinese interlocutors, both on diplomatic as well as the military levels through meeting with military commanders at various levels. These discussions had in the past resulted in the resolution of standoffs at various locations. There are some locations and areas where stand-offs had not been resolved," said Misri. "Now, as a result of the discussions taking place over the last several weeks an agreement has been arrived at on patrolling arrangements along the LAC in the India - China border areas. This is leading to disengagement and eventually a resolution of the issues that had arisen in these areas in 2020," he added. (ANI)

items.title: Mukka Proteins Limited Announces Rs 98 Crore Preferential Issue for Acquisition and Expansion
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel VMPL Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 22: Mukka Proteins Limited , India's largest fish meal and insect meal producer and a leader in the animal protein industry , has announced the approval of a preferential issue worth Rs 98 crore by its Board of Directors. This strategic move will help Mukka Proteins in its ongoing domestic and international acquisition and expansion efforts, reinforcing its position in the global market. A significant portion of the funding will come from the promoter and promoter group, underlining their commitment to the company's robust growth strategy. The preferential issue will comprise up to 1.96 crore equity shares at Rs50 per share, aggregating to Rs98 crore. This price includes a premium of Rs49 per share on the face value of Rs1. Mukka Proteins will use the raised capital to enhance production capabilities and meet the growing global demand for sustainable and high-quality protein solutions, particularly in the fishmeal and insect meal sectors. In a clear show of confidence, Mukka Proteins' promoters have committed to a capital infusion of INR 60 crore through a preferential allotment of equity shares. This significant financial backing will be used to strengthen the company's financial position, reduce debt, and fund key operational improvements. Mukka Proteins has consistently embraced sustainability, having commercialized insect protein as a significant innovation for the aquaculture and animal feed industry. The company's waste-to-food initiatives have contributed to environmental sustainability, particularly in collaboration with the Mangaluru municipality for waste management. These efforts not only align with global environmental best practices but also enhance circular economy processes, focusing on converting municipal waste into valuable protein and oil products. Mukka Proteins is known for its strong commitment to ecological preservation, evident through the development of sustainable products such as fishmeal, fish oil, and insect protein. As a key player in the aquaculture and nutraceutical markets, Mukka contributes 25-30% of the market share in India's fishmeal and fish oil industry. The company plans to expand its operations further, capitalizing on this capital infusion to enter new markets and enhance its global footprint.

This issuance is subject to necessary statutory and regulatory approvals, including shareholder approval at the upcoming Extra-Ordinary General Meeting (EGM) on November 16, 2024. Managing Director and CEO Harris commented, "This preferential issue is a major milestone for Mukka Proteins as we continue to strengthen our market position. Our growth plans remain firmly rooted in sustainability, and this capital will enable us to scale up production, diversify our product offerings, and reinforce our commitment to responsible and eco-friendly business practices." Mukka Proteins Limited is poised to capture new opportunities in the animal protein sector, reinforcing its legacy of innovation, sustainability, and operational excellence. Mukka Proteins Limited : Mukka Proteins Limited is a leading manufacturer and exporter of fish meal , fish oil, and other protein products. The company has built a reputation for delivering high-quality, sustainable protein products to a global customer base. With a commitment to innovation and quality, Mukka Proteins serves industries including aquaculture, pet food, and agriculture across multiple continents. Headquartered in Mangalore, India, Mukka Proteins operates state-of-the-art processing facilities that meet stringent international standards. The company is dedicated to sustainable practices and has been at the forefront of environmental stewardship within the protein processing industry. items.title: India to grow at 6.8 pc in FY25 and 6.6 pc in FY26: S&P Global Market Intelligence
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): India's growth, although moderating, remains strong with a forecasted average of 6.8 per cent for the fiscal year 2024-25 and 6.6 per cent for 2025-26, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence . Despite a slowdown in economic momentum due to weaker public-sector investment, the outlook for India's economy is buoyed by several positive factors. Easing inflation, favourable monsoon conditions, and increased government social spending are expected to boost household demand. Additionally, healthy corporate balance sheets are playing a vital role in supporting the recovery of private investment. S&P Global Market Intelligence has released its October Global Economic Forecast update, emphasizing a steady global economic expansion supported by policy stimulus, while acknowledging risks from geopolitical factors. The outlook highlights moderating inflation and easing monetary policies as key factors steering the global economy towards a "soft landing."

Ken Wattret, global economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence , remarked, "The global economy is on track for a soft landing, with inflation rates moderating and monetary policy easing becoming more widespread. Still, geopolitical developments have the capacity to dampen or even derail the expansion." Report forecasts an annual real GDP growth rate of 4.3 per cent in 2024 and 4.4 per cent in 2025 for the region excluding China and Japan. Aiding this growth is resilient domestic demand, as regional central banks adopt more accommodative monetary stances. The start of the US Federal Reserve's easing cycle in September is creating more room for interest rate cuts, prompting several central banks, including those in the Philippines, New Zealand, Hong Kong SAR, and Indonesia, to lower rates. S&P Global Market Intelligence underscores that while the global economic outlook remains positive, risks persist. Geopolitical tensions could potentially derail economic progress, especially in regions with heightened uncertainties. Nonetheless, policy measures aimed at stimulating growth, coupled with moderating inflation, are setting the stage for a sustained economic expansion. (ANI)

items.title: Who has won all four Grand Slams and the ATP Finals? Agassi, Federer, Djokovic and now Alcaraz
paras: By beating Alexander Zverev in the 2026 ATP Finals final in Turin, Carlos Alcaraz became the fourth man to have won the Australian Open, Roland-Garros, Wimbledon, the US Open and the season-ending championship, after Andre Agassi, Roger Federer and Novak Djokovic.
Here is everything about this exclusive club, from the dates and ages to the legends who missed out.

Only four men have won all five of the biggest titles in men’s tennis: the four Grand Slam tournaments and the ATP Finals. They are Andre Agassi , Roger Federer , Novak Djokovic and, since November 22, 2026, Carlos Alcaraz , who beat Alexander Zverev 6-2, 7-6(7) in the final in Turin . Alcaraz is also by far the youngest member of the club: he completed the set at 23 years and 6 months, more than four years younger than Federer, the next youngest.

items.title: Every word Carlos Alcaraz said after winning the ATP Finals including his message for Alexander Zverev
paras: Carlos Alcaraz is the new champion of the ATP Finals after a hard-fought victory over Alexander Zverev. Alcaraz loves playing in front of Italian tennis fans , who have just witnessed the Spaniard clinch the ATP Finals title in Turin for the very first time.

He defeated Zverev 6-2, 7-6(9-7) in an entertaining final, which lasted just over two hours. Zverev has made huge strides this season , but the world number one couldn’t cap off his stunning 2026 by claiming a third ATP Finals success.

Instead, his Spanish rival has lifted the trophy for the first time in his career, going one step further than his runner-up finish in 2025. Alcaraz has now reacted to his superb success, which represents the sixth ATP title of his extraordinary campaign. How many majors will Carlos Alcaraz win next year?

items.title: Head, Heart And Balls: Carlos Alcaraz Follows Grandpa’s Advice To Win First ATP Finals Title
paras: Carlos Alcaraz has ended Spain’s 28-year wait for an ATP Finals champion after dismissing a misfiring Alexander Zverev in straight sets. The Spaniard battled his way to a 6-2, 7-6(7) win over an out-of-sorts Zverev, who produced 31 unforced errors compared to 12 winners.

Alcaraz, who is currently on a 14-match winning streak, has become only the fourth player in history to have won every Grand Slam event and the ATP Finals. Andre Agassi, Roger Federer and Novak Djokovic are the others to have achieved this milestone.

Alcaraz showed no sign of physical issues throughout the final. Earlier in the tournament, he had a hamstring issue and underwent an MRI to check for damage. He was wearing taping around his upper left leg and right knee, as he had in his previous match.

Friendships are built by repeated contact, not by being liked
items.hook: This is the single most useful fact in the whole guide.
paras: Studies of primary-school classrooms found that children seated next to each other were far more likely to become friends than children seated across the room. When teachers changed the seating, new friendships formed with the new neighbours.

So the engine is: same place, same people, same activity, over and over. The day at the yo-yo bar followed by basketball is that engine working - shared activity changed how the other boy treated him. It was not luck.
items.do: Pick one activity he already likes and commit to it weekly for a full term.

items.title: Keep the proximity - change the watching
items.hook: Your instinct is half right, and the other half matters.
paras: You are right that being around the group matters: children nominate as friends the children they see and interact with most. 'Out of sight, out of mind' is real for acquaintances.

But guidance written for schools is blunt: merely remaining beside a group is not friendship. A child who hovers is read as a bystander rather than a player, and it holds him in the one-down position. Watching has a use - but only as the first twenty seconds of joining in, never as the endpoint.
items.do: Keep telling him to stay near the group. Add: 'then take a job in the game'.

items.title: Teach 'watch, then blend'
items.hook: The best way to join a game is not to ask.
paras: Most of us were told to walk up and say 'Can I play?' But that makes everyone stop and look at him, and makes 'no' very easy.

The better sequence, used by people who study play: watch for about twenty seconds to learn the game and where the line is, then slide into the action without stopping it. Take the end of the line. Stand in the outfield. Pick up the ball and pass it back.
items.do: Rehearse it at home in five minutes. Ask him to name the 'easiest job' in each game.

items.title: Host one friend at a time - this is the biggest lever you control
items.hook: The child who invites is rarely short of friends.
paras: Pick a child he has had fun with in the last month, not someone he admires from afar. Invite one person for one to two hours. Put away anything precious, have two activities ready, start with a snack, and let the guest choose sometimes.
Keep it short and end while they are both still enjoying it. Then leave a few weeks before inviting the same child again, so the invitation can come back to him.
items.do: Text one parent this week and set a date for the school holidays.

items.title: Ask the teacher one specific question
items.hook: Teachers see the playground. Ask them to name names.
paras: Ask two things: who does he play well with, and could he be seated near them or paired with them for group work?
Seating is one of the few levers that reliably creates new friendships, and it is invisible to the children - no one has to know it was arranged.
items.do: Email the teacher this week with those two questions.

items.title: Do not push into a group that is rejecting him
items.hook: Here the advice is the opposite of persistence.
paras: Where a group is actively excluding him, the guidance is to back off - when you back off from people, they can move towards you. Put his energy into two or three other children instead of one closed circle.
Friends in more than one place - school, a club, family friends - also make him far less vulnerable when one group turns cold.
items.do: Help him list three children outside the difficult group he could get to know.

items.title: One or two good friends is the goal - not popularity
paras: Kids need one or two good friends. You do not need to worry about him being the most popular child in the class.
His warmth and kindness are already the raw material. Treat this as coaching a skill, not fixing a fault - if he feels like a project, he will resist.
items.do: Say his strengths out loud, often. Confidence is what carries a child into a group.

items.title: Playing and talking with girls is normal and good
items.hook: Children believe gender matters far more than it actually does.
paras: In one large classroom experiment, simply seating boys and girls next to each other doubled how often they became friends.
Girls' play tends to build conversation, turn-taking and inventing games together; boys' play builds bigger, faster group play. Being good at both widens his circle.
items.do: No action needed. Just do not let him think it is odd.

items.title: When to get more help
items.hook: Ordinary friendship difficulty is not a disorder.
paras: Get more support if he becomes reluctant to go to school, is persistently distressed, has changes in sleep or appetite, or says it is happening all the time and he cannot make it stop.
Start with his teacher, then the school counsellor, then your GP for a referral. Kids Helpline is free and open 24/7 on 1800 55 1800, for children and for parents.
items.do: Save Kids Helpline in your phone: 1800 55 1800.
